## Rewritten build prompt

```text
Build a complete, production-ready, client-side web application that provides an asset-selection and image-library interface, including all user-facing screens, dialogs, controls, responsive layouts, interaction states, keyboard accessibility, persistence, validation, and error handling.

Deliver the full implementation as one self-contained `index.html` file. Put all HTML, CSS, JavaScript, SVG icons, templates, application state management, routing, modal logic, search, filtering, sorting, selection, deletion workflows, and responsive behavior inside that single file. Do not create separate frontend files, build steps, package manifests, external JavaScript modules, mock records, placeholder content, simulated functionality, or incomplete components. Do not require a framework, bundler, transpiler, server runtime, or installation step. The file must run by opening it in a modern browser.

Construct the application as follows.

1. Create a responsive application shell with a polished, high-density asset-library layout. Support desktop, tablet, phablet, and mobile viewport widths. Use semantic HTML elements where appropriate and maintain a consistent visual system across every screen: neutral background colors, compact typography, subtle borders, rounded controls, distinct focus rings, hover states, disabled states, selected states, active states, destructive-action styling, and clear contrast for all interactive components.

2. Implement an asset-selection modal dialog that opens above the application content. Use a real accessible dialog pattern with:
   - A modal backdrop that blocks pointer interaction with the page behind it.
   - Focus trapping while the modal is open.
   - Escape-key dismissal.
   - A visible close button in the upper-right corner.
   - Restored focus to the triggering element after the modal closes.
   - `aria-modal="true"`, an accessible dialog name, and descriptive labels for all controls.
   - Mobile-specific sizing and layout behavior so the dialog occupies the usable viewport without clipping controls.

3. Set the modal title to “Select assets to add”. Place a compact close button alongside the title. Use an inline SVG “X” icon for the close control. Do not rely on icon fonts or remote image assets.

4. Add a top control area inside the asset-selection dialog:
   - A search input with a magnifying-glass SVG icon.
   - Placeholder text: “Search for an image...”.
   - Case-insensitive search across asset filenames and asset classifications.
   - Immediate filtering as the user types.
   - A segmented scope toggle labeled for assistive technology as “Show all assets or originals only”.
   - Two scope options: “All” and “Originals”.
   - “All” must display every asset.
   - “Originals” must exclude processed or edited-output assets and display only source assets.
   - Clearly style the active scope option.
   - Include an icon-only sort control with an accessible label of “Sort options”.
   - When activated, show a keyboard-accessible menu with at least filename ascending, filename descending, newest first, and oldest first options.
   - Display the selected sorting mode in the control’s accessible state and apply sorting immediately.

5. Build the main asset area as a responsive asset grid. On narrow mobile layouts, display a single column. Increase the number of columns progressively as viewport width increases. Each asset card must include:
   - A selectable visual thumbnail region.
   - A keyboard-focusable selection control with an accessible label of “Select”.
   - A visible selection overlay or check indicator when selected.
   - An actual asset preview generated from the asset’s own browser-managed image data whenever available.
   - A deterministic fallback preview generated in-browser when image preview rendering fails, using the asset filename or intrinsic file information rather than decorative dummy graphics.
   - A filename title using the full original filename as a tooltip and an ellipsized visible label where necessary.
   - A classification label, such as “Source image” or “Edited output”.
   - Support for image names including:
     - `75378160659__D21B4668-8FBB-49A2-AFA4-12A2070B16C3.jpeg`
     - `IMG_2609.jpeg`
     - `0595D034-AC18-4A2A-A0A8-C7C1A688112B--3915800780350463956.jpeg`
     - `IMG_0600.png`
     - `IMG_8325_Original.jpeg`
     - `image.png`
     - `IMG_9957.png`
     - `image 29.jpeg`
     - `source.jpeg`
     - `IMG_9948.jpeg`
   - Correct handling of repeated filenames as separate asset records with unique internal identifiers.

6. Provide a fully functional selection workflow:
   - Clicking or pressing Enter or Space on an asset selection control toggles that individual asset.
   - Support selecting multiple assets simultaneously.
   - Maintain selection state while searching, changing scope, changing sort order, opening menus, and resizing the viewport.
   - Add a persistent modal footer with a selected-item count.
   - Add a secondary “Cancel” control that closes the selector without committing changes.
   - Add a primary “Add selected assets” control that commits the currently selected assets to the application’s main asset collection.
   - Disable the primary add control if no asset is selected.
   - Ensure that adding selected assets does not duplicate records already added unless the user has explicitly removed those records and selects them again.

7. Create a main application asset-library view behind the selector. It must show the collection of added assets and expose an action that opens the “Select assets to add” dialog. The main asset-library view must:
   - Render added assets in a responsive grid.
   - Retain asset filenames, classifications, creation timestamps, and unique identifiers.
   - Store application state locally in browser storage so reloads preserve assets, selections where appropriate, sort preferences, and interface preferences.
   - Offer a search field for the main library.
   - Offer filtering between all assets, source images, and edited outputs.
   - Provide an empty state only when the real stored library contains no assets, with an action to open the selector.
   - Use actual uploaded or browser-supplied images where available; do not invent image files or fake upload outcomes.

8. Provide asset deletion in the main library. Every asset card must expose a delete action. When deletion is requested:
   - Open a confirmation dialog with the heading “Deleting file”.
   - Include a close button in the dialog header.
   - Display a confirmation question in this exact pattern: `Are you sure you want to delete 'FILENAME'?`
   - Display the warning text: “Any edited versions of that file will also be deleted.”
   - Include a secondary button labeled “Keep”.
   - Include a destructive primary button labeled “Delete”.
   - “Keep” and the close control must cancel deletion.
   - “Delete” must remove the targeted source asset and every edited-output asset that identifies that source asset as its parent.
   - Remove deleted records from browser storage immediately.
   - Close the confirmation dialog after deletion.
   - Restore focus to the delete trigger that opened the dialog when deletion is canceled; when deletion succeeds, move focus to the next logical asset action or the library heading.

9. Support real local asset ingestion:
   - Include a visible local-file import action in the main application view.
   - Accept common image formats supported by the browser, including PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF, and SVG where browser rendering allows.
   - Read selected files using the browser File API.
   - Generate object URLs or data URLs for local preview.
   - Capture real filename, MIME type, file size, last-modified timestamp, image dimensions when available, import timestamp, original-versus-output classification, and source-parent relationship where applicable.
   - Reject unreadable or unsupported files with an explicit error message.
   - Preserve import data in browser storage when technically possible; if browser storage capacity prevents persistence of file payloads, preserve metadata and communicate the persistence limitation in the application interface without losing the current session’s usable asset preview.
   - Do not claim a file was uploaded, saved remotely, processed, edited, or transformed when it has not been.

10. Implement edited-output relationships as real internal data relationships:
   - Every asset record must include a unique ID, filename, asset kind, created timestamp, and optional `sourceAssetId`.
   - Asset kinds must include at least `source` and `edited-output`.
   - The “Originals” selector scope must show only records whose asset kind is `source`.
   - The deletion confirmation warning must be operational: deleting a source record must delete all records whose `sourceAssetId` equals the source record’s ID, including all descendants if the data model permits nested relationships.
   - If an edited-output record is deleted individually, delete only that output unless the user targeted its source record.

11. Add robust empty, loading, error, and no-results states:
   - Show a loading indicator only during actual asynchronous browser work, such as FileReader or image-dimension extraction.
   - Show “No assets match your search” when filtering returns no results.
   - Show a clear import error when a file cannot be parsed.
   - Show a clear storage error when browser persistence fails.
   - Do not display artificial loading spinners, fake task progress, mock thumbnails, invented cloud status, or fabricated file metadata.

12. Implement all interaction details:
   - Clicking outside a modal backdrop must close non-destructive dialogs only when doing so cannot discard uncommitted selection changes without a clear cancellation policy. The deletion confirmation dialog must not delete on backdrop click.
   - Use event delegation or modular functions for repeated card actions.
   - Prevent duplicate event handlers after rerendering.
   - Keep DOM updates efficient by rendering only the affected grid and modal regions where practical.
   - Use a centralized JavaScript state object, with explicit functions for loading state, saving state, generating unique IDs, importing files, selecting assets, filtering, sorting, opening dialogs, closing dialogs, confirming deletion, and rerendering UI regions.
   - Sanitize filename-derived text before inserting it into the DOM. Use `textContent` rather than unsafe HTML interpolation for user-provided names.
   - Validate all data restored from browser storage before rendering it.
   - Avoid unsafe use of `innerHTML` for dynamic file metadata and filenames.

13. Implement keyboard and accessibility support across the application:
   - All controls must be reachable through Tab navigation.
   - Interactive non-button elements must have correct roles, keyboard operations, labels, and pressed or selected state semantics.
   - The asset selection checkbox controls must expose `aria-pressed` or equivalent checked-state semantics.
   - The scope toggle must expose its group label and active option.
   - The sort menu must use appropriate menu or listbox semantics, support Arrow Up, Arrow Down, Home, End, Enter, Space, and Escape, and return focus to its trigger when dismissed.
   - Modal dialogs must have visible headings referenced through `aria-labelledby`.
   - Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.
   - Ensure focus indicators remain visible on every background and control state.

14. Build a coherent visual language:
   - Use a lightweight system font stack.
   - Keep controls compact and touch-friendly.
   - Use subtle card borders and thumbnail containers.
   - Make selected assets visibly distinguishable without obscuring the preview.
   - Use a neutral secondary-button style for “Keep” and a visually distinct destructive style for “Delete”.
   - Use CSS custom properties for color, spacing, radius, shadow, typography, breakpoints, and transition duration.
   - Include dark-mode support using `prefers-color-scheme`, with appropriate contrast and legibility.
   - Keep the application usable from approximately 320px wide mobile screens through large desktop screens.

15. Include a final in-file quality check through executable behavior, not comments:
   - On initial launch, render the persisted real library if browser storage contains valid data.
   - If no valid data exists, render the real empty-library state and enable local import.
   - Verify that importing a real image creates a usable asset card.
   - Verify that search, scope filtering, sorting, asset selection, add-to-library behavior, deletion confirmation, cascading deletion, dialog closing, keyboard navigation, and browser-storage persistence work without external services.
   - Ensure the document contains no references to an existing software product, no external dependency URLs, no remote tracking scripts, no framework bootstrap code, no placeholder records, and no incomplete features.

Return the complete, unabridged contents of the single `index.html` file and nothing else.
```

The supplied technical material describes an image-asset selection interface with searchable asset cards, an “All”/“Originals” scope switch, sort control, source-image classification, and a destructive deletion confirmation that warns related edited versions will also be deleted.[1]
